title: Sindbad the Sailor: Third Voyage
paragraphs: After a very short time, the easy, pleasant life I led made me forget the dangers of my first two voyages. And since I was still in the prime of life, I preferred to be up and doing. So I gathered the rarest and finest merchandise Baghdad had to offer, took it to Balsora, and set sail with other merchants I knew, bound for distant lands. We had called at many ports and made a good deal of profit when, one day on the open sea, a terrible wind caught us and blew us far off our course. It lasted for several days and finally drove us into a harbor on a strange island.

“I would rather have dropped anchor anywhere than here,” our captain said. “This island, and all the ones near it, are inhabited by hairy savages, and they are certain to attack us. Whatever these dwarfs do, we dare not fight back. They swarm like locusts, and if we kill even one of them, the rest will fall on us and finish us off in no time.”

These words threw the whole ship’s company into great alarm, and we soon found out that the captain had told the truth. A vast crowd of hideous savages appeared, no more than two feet tall and covered in reddish fur. They threw themselves into the waves and surrounded our vessel. Chattering all the while in a language we could not understand, they grabbed at ropes and gangways and swarmed up the ship’s side so fast and so nimbly that they almost seemed to fly.

You can imagine the rage and terror that gripped us as we watched them, not daring to stop them and unable to say a word to turn them from their purpose, whatever it was. We were not left in doubt for long. They hoisted the sails and cut the anchor cable, and sailed our ship to another island a little farther off, where they forced us ashore. Then they took the ship and went back to the place they had come from, leaving us helpless on a shore that all sailors avoid in horror, for a reason you will soon learn.

We turned away from the sea and trudged miserably inland. On the way we found herbs and fruits and ate them, feeling that since we had to die we might as well put it off as long as we could, though we had no hope of getting away. After a while, far in the distance, we saw what looked like a magnificent palace, and we dragged our tired feet toward it. When we came up to it, though, we found it was really a castle, tall and solidly built. We pushed open its heavy ebony doors and walked into the courtyard, but at the entrance to the great hall beyond we stopped dead, frozen with horror at what lay before us. On one side was a huge heap of bones—human bones—and on the other were countless spits for roasting! Overcome with despair, we collapsed trembling on the ground and lay there, unable to speak or move. The sun was going down when a loud crash woke us. The door of the hall was flung violently open, and a hideous giant came in. He was as tall as a palm tree and completely black, with a single eye that blazed like a burning coal in the middle of his forehead. His teeth were long and sharp, and they stuck out in a dreadful grin. His lower lip hung down onto his chest, his ears were like an elephant’s and covered his shoulders, and his nails were like the claws of some savage bird.

The sight was so terrible that we lost our senses and lay there like dead men. When we finally came round, the giant was sitting and studying us closely with his fearful eye. After he had looked at us long enough, he came over, reached out his hand and picked me up by the back of the neck. He turned me over this way and that, but when he felt that I was nothing but skin and bone, he put me down again and went on to the next man, and handled him the same way. At last he got to the captain, and since he was the fattest of us all, the giant lifted him in one hand, stuck him on a spit and built up an enormous fire, where he roasted him. When the giant had finished his supper, he lay down to sleep and snored as loud as thunder. We lay shivering with horror all night long, and when day broke he woke up and went out, leaving us in the castle.

When we were sure he had really gone, we jumped up and wailed over our dreadful fate until the hall rang with our cries of despair. There were many of us and only one of him, yet it never crossed our minds to kill him. Even if we had thought of it, it would have been a hard thing to do, and we could not think of any plan to free ourselves. So at last, giving in to our miserable lot, we spent the day wandering about the island, eating whatever fruit we could find, and when night came we went back to the castle, since we had looked everywhere for another shelter and found none. At sunset the giant came back, ate one of our poor companions for supper, slept and snored until dawn, and left us as he had the day before. Our situation seemed so horrible that several of my companions thought it would be better to throw themselves off the cliffs and die in the waves right away than to wait for such a wretched end. But I had a plan of escape, and I now explained it to them, and they agreed at once to try it.

“Listen, my brothers,” I said. “You know there is plenty of driftwood along the shore. Let’s build several rafts and carry them to a good spot. If our plot works, we can wait patiently for a ship to pass and rescue us from this deadly island. If it fails, we’ll have to take to the rafts quickly. Flimsy as they are, we have a better chance of saving our lives on them than we do by staying here.”

They all agreed, and we spent the day building rafts, each big enough for three people. At nightfall we went back to the castle, and soon the giant came in, and one more of us was sacrificed. But the time for our revenge was close! As soon as he had finished his horrible meal he lay down to sleep as before. When we heard him begin to snore, I and nine of the boldest of my comrades got up quietly. Each of us took a spit and heated it red-hot in the fire, and at a signal we all drove them together into the giant’s eye, blinding him completely. He gave a terrible cry and leapt to his feet, grabbing wildly in every direction to catch one of us. But as soon as the deed was done we had all run off different ways and thrown ourselves flat on the ground in corners where he was unlikely to step on us.

After searching in vain, he groped around until he found the door and ran out of it, howling dreadfully. As for us, once he was gone we hurried out of the cursed castle and stationed ourselves beside our rafts to see what would happen. Our thinking was this: if, when the sun rose, there was no sign of the giant and we no longer heard his howls, which were still reaching us faintly through the darkness and growing more and more distant, we would take it that he was dead, and we could safely stay on the island without risking our lives on the flimsy rafts. But alas! In the morning light we saw our enemy coming toward us, held up on each side by a giant almost as huge and terrible as himself, with a crowd more following right behind them. We didn’t hesitate any longer. We scrambled onto our rafts and rowed out to sea with all our strength. The giants saw their prey escaping, so they snatched up enormous chunks of rock, waded into the water and hurled them after us. They aimed so well that every raft except mine was swamped, and the unlucky men on them drowned, with nothing we could do to help. Even I and my two companions had all we could manage to keep our raft out of the giants’ reach, but by rowing hard we finally got out to open sea. There the winds and waves had us at their mercy and tossed us about all that day and night, but the next morning we found ourselves near an island, and we landed gladly.

We found delicious fruit there, and when we had eaten our fill we lay down to rest on the shore. Suddenly a loud rustling woke us. We jumped up and saw that it came from an enormous snake sliding toward us across the sand. It moved so fast that it had caught one of my companions before he could run, and despite his cries and struggles it quickly crushed the life out of him in its powerful coils and began to swallow him. By then my other companion and I were running for our lives, looking for some place safe from this new horror. We saw a tall tree and climbed into it, after first gathering a supply of fruit from the bushes nearby. When night came I fell asleep, only to be woken once more by the terrible snake. It hissed horribly around the tree and at last reared up against it, and finding my sleeping companion perched just below me, it swallowed him too and crawled away, leaving me half dead with terror.

When the sun rose I crept down from the tree. I had hardly any hope of escaping the dreadful fate that had overtaken my comrades, but life is sweet, and I was determined to do everything I could to save myself. All day long I worked in a frantic hurry, gathering heaps of dry brushwood, reeds and thorns and tying them into bundles. I made a ring of them around my tree and piled them firmly one on top of another until I had a sort of tent, where I crouched like a mouse in its hole when it sees the cat coming. You can imagine what a fearful night I spent, for the snake came back, eager to devour me, and slid round and round my flimsy shelter looking for a way in. Every moment I feared it would manage to shove some of the bundles aside, but luckily for me they held together, and when it grew light my enemy slunk back to its den, baffled and hungry. As for me, I was more dead than alive! Shaking with fright and half choked by the monster’s poisonous breath, I came out of my tent and crawled down to the sea. I felt it would be better to jump off the cliffs and end my life at once than to live through another night like that. But then, to my joy and relief, I saw a ship sailing past, and by shouting wildly and waving my turban I managed to catch the attention of her crew.

They sent a boat to pick me up, and soon I was on board, surrounded by a crowd of astonished sailors and merchants, all eager to know how I had come to be on that deserted island. When I had told my story they gave me the best food the ship had to offer, and the captain, seeing that I was in rags, kindly gave me one of his own coats. We sailed on for some time and called at many ports, until at last we came to the island of Salahat, where sandal wood grows in great quantities. We dropped anchor there, and I was standing watching the merchants unload their goods and get ready to sell or trade them, when the captain came up to me and said,

“Brother, I have some merchandise here that belonged to a passenger of mine who died. Would you do me the favor of trading with it? When I meet his heirs I’ll be able to give them the money, though it’s only fair that you should have a share for your trouble.”

I agreed gladly, since I didn’t like standing around doing nothing. He then showed me the bales and sent for the man whose job it was to keep the list of goods on board. When this man arrived, he asked under what name the merchandise should be entered.
“Under the name of Sindbad the Sailor,” the captain answered.

I was greatly startled at this, but when I looked at him carefully I recognized him as the captain of the ship I had sailed on for my second voyage, though he had changed a great deal since then. He believed me to be dead, so it was no wonder that he had not recognized me.
“So, captain,” I said, “the merchant who owned those bales was called Sindbad?”

“Yes,” he replied. “That was his name. He came from Baghdad and joined my ship at Balsora. But by bad luck he got left behind on a desert island where we had put in to fill our water-casks, and it was four hours before anyone noticed he was missing. By then the wind had picked up, and we couldn’t turn back for him.”
“So you think he died?” I asked.
“Alas, yes,” he answered.
“Why, captain!” I cried. “Take a good look at me. I am that Sindbad, who fell asleep on the island and woke to find himself abandoned!”
The captain stared at me in amazement, but before long he was convinced that I was telling the truth, and he was overjoyed that I had escaped.
“At least I can now get that piece of carelessness off my conscience,” he said. “Take your goods, and the profit I’ve made on them for you, and may you do well from now on.”

I took them gratefully, and as we sailed from island to island I bought up supplies of cloves, cinnamon and other spices. In one place I saw a tortoise twenty cubits long and just as wide, and a fish that looked like a cow, with skin so thick that it was used to make shields. I saw another creature that was like a camel in shape and color. So, bit by bit, we made our way back to Balsora, and I went home to Baghdad with so much money that I couldn’t count it myself, besides endless treasures. I gave generously to the poor and bought a lot more land to add to what I already owned, and that was the end of my third voyage.

When Sindbad had finished his story, he gave Hindbad another hundred sequins, and Hindbad left with the other guests. The next day, when they had all gathered again and the banquet was over, their host went on with his adventures.
